chapter: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
title: Freddie Keppard's tin cans, flutter-tongue and technique
summary: Briggs describes Keppard as a technical freak player with tin-can effects, flutter-tongue, half-valves, a sharp attack and fast technique, and notes how high trumpet ranges were regarded then.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Well, what was Keppard's playing like? What was his playing like?
Keppard, I think that he was curious. He invented, more or less, the system of using tin cans and that sort of thing on his bell, to get different sounds, you see.
He would use what, a tin can?
A tin can, yes.
Water drinking glass, water glass?
Oh yes, yes. But more or less a tin can. He had a series of them, large, small, and for different effects, you see.
Briggs
I see.
And his flutter-tongue, that was the first time I heard a flutter-tongue.
Well, was that a real flutter-tongue or a growl?
It was a flutter-tongue.
A flutter-tongue.
A flutter-tongue or growl (Laughter).
But with throat tones, he was making them with throat tones, was he?
Yes, some of them tones, yes. He was what you'd call a freak.
A freak player?
A freak player.
He used half-valves, as most of them use anyhow, at times, you know, to get that half wierd tone.
And he was simply terrific, because
Briggs
he had a wonderful attack.
Very sharp.
Very sharp. Oh, very sharp, but solid. He led the band, he was solid as a rock.
He and Bechet, I mean, it was a solid band.
Okay, I'd like to just stay with this a little bit.
The records that I've heard of Keppard were made later, all of them were made later, I mean, I'm talking about '26, around that time.
Yes.
He was playing an awful lot of quarter notes and not so many eighth notes.
Yes, I understand, Yes. I don't know, I never heard any of his recordings. I was in Europe.
Well, was he playing more eighth notes when you heard him?
Briggs
Well, played quite a lot. He played a -- he had a good foundation of technique.
Fast?
Very fast. Very fast.

He was not -- I don't know whether he was a good reader, but it seems that he must have been a good reader, 'cause the control that he had of his instrument, just speaking of his instrument, was simply terrific.
He must have been a good reader in order to have been able to execute the way he did.
A good high register?
Pretty good.
What would you say, could he make a good --
Well, in those days, trumpets very seldom climbed to high C, in those days.
So high C was high?
Briggs 74
Yes, it was pretty high. A guy makes an A, he was pretty good, and a B-flat was better, you know. And if you ever make a top C, then you just, you know.
The high register wasn't so -- I mean many people didn't think -- been tried to (?)
Right.
But I heard a trumpet player, I don't remember his name, I try to get his name, at the Elite Number 1. He made a high B-flat while I was there and I thought it was heaven.
